title: Given a Scenario, Apply Security Best Practices

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud security is strongest when systems are designed securely from the beginning and continuously maintained.
CompTIA wants you to recognize practices that reduce trust, minimize exposure, protect data, secure credentials, and limit unnecessary permissions.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: What security practice reduces the specific risk in the scenario?
sections.callout: Reduce trust → Zero Trust. Secure configuration → benchmark or hardening. Fix a vulnerability → patching. Protect data → encryption. Limit access → least privilege. Protect credentials → secrets management.

sections.title: Zero Trust
paragraphs: Zero Trust assumes that no user, system, or connection should automatically be trusted simply because of location or previous access.
Access should be explicitly verified. Think: Never trust automatically; verify access.
sections.callout: Internal location should not automatically grant trust → Zero Trust.

sections.title: Security Benchmarks
paragraphs: A benchmark provides recommended secure configuration settings.

entries.title: Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmark
paragraphs: The Center for Internet Security publishes security configuration benchmarks for many technologies.
Think: Independent secure configuration baseline.
entries.recognitionCue: The organization needs standardized secure configuration guidance → CIS benchmark.

entries.title: Vendor-Specific Benchmark
paragraphs: Cloud and technology vendors may publish security recommendations specifically for their own platforms.
Think: The manufacturer tells you how to securely configure its product.
entries.recognitionCue: Guidance is specifically tailored to one provider or product → vendor-specific benchmark.

sections.title: Hardening
paragraphs: Hardening reduces the attack surface by securely configuring the system.
Examples include disabling unnecessary services, removing unnecessary accounts, closing unused ports, and applying secure configuration settings.
Think: Remove everything the attacker does not need you to leave open.
sections.callout: Unnecessary functionality is being removed or locked down → hardening.

sections.title: Patching
paragraphs: Patching fixes known software vulnerabilities and defects.
sections.callout: A known software flaw needs correction → patching.

entries.title: Data in Transit
paragraphs: Data in transit is information moving between systems. Encryption protects that information while it crosses networks.
Think: Protect data while traveling.
entries.recognitionCue: Information must be protected while moving → encryption in transit.

entries.title: Data at Rest
paragraphs: Data at rest is stored information, including databases, storage volumes, files, and backups.
Think: Protect data while sitting still.
entries.recognitionCue: Stored information must be protected → encryption at rest.

sections.title: Secrets Management
paragraphs: Secrets include sensitive credentials used by users, systems, and applications, such as passwords, API keys, tokens, and encryption keys.
Secrets management stores and controls these values securely rather than embedding them directly into application code.
Think: Do not hard-code the keys to the kingdom.
sections.callout: API keys or passwords should not appear in source code → secrets management.

sections.title: API Security
paragraphs: APIs expose functions and data to other systems.
API security ensures those interfaces are properly authenticated, authorized, protected, and restricted.
Think: An API is a door. Secure the door.
sections.callout: Attackers could misuse an application interface → API security.

sections.title: Principle of Least Privilege
paragraphs: The principle of least privilege grants only the minimum access required to perform a job.
Think: Give exactly enough permission—and no more.
sections.callout: A user or application has excessive permissions → least privilege.

entries.title: Privileged Containers
paragraphs: A privileged container has elevated permissions and greater access to underlying host capabilities. That increased power creates increased risk.
Think: A container with the master keys.
entries.recognitionCue: A container has extensive host-level permissions → privileged container.

entries.title: Unprivileged Containers
paragraphs: An unprivileged container runs with limited permissions. This reduces the damage the container may cause if compromised.
Think: A container gets only what it actually needs.
entries.recognitionCue: Container privileges should be minimized → unprivileged container.

entries.title: File Access Permissions
paragraphs: Container files and mounted resources should have appropriate permissions.
Think: A container should not read or modify files it has no business touching.
entries.recognitionCue: The issue concerns who can access container files → file access permissions.

entries.title: Object Storage Security
paragraphs: Object storage access must be restricted so unauthorized users cannot retrieve or modify stored objects.
Think: A cloud bucket should not become public because of an incorrect access setting.
entries.recognitionCue: Cloud objects are unintentionally publicly accessible → object storage security.

entries.title: File Storage Security
paragraphs: File storage security controls who can access shared files and directories.
entries.recognitionCue: Permissions on shared files or folders are the issue → file storage security.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Do not trust based on location → Zero Trust
Standard secure configuration guidance → CIS
Provider-specific security recommendation → Vendor-specific benchmark
Disable unnecessary services → Hardening
Fix a known vulnerability → Patching
Protect traffic → Encryption in transit
Protect stored information → Encryption at rest
Protect API keys or passwords → Secrets management
Secure an exposed service interface → API security
Minimum permissions → Principle of least privilege
Container has elevated host access → Privileged
Restrict container rights → Unprivileged
Restrict container files → File access permissions
Restrict object access → Object storage security
Restrict shared file access → File storage security

entries.title: Hardening vs. Patching
paragraphs: Hardening reduces exposure through configuration. Patching fixes software flaws.

entries.title: Encryption at Rest vs. In Transit
paragraphs: Moving data is in transit. Stored data is at rest.

entries.title: Least Privilege vs. Zero Trust
paragraphs: Least privilege says to grant minimum permissions. Zero Trust says not to trust automatically and to verify access explicitly. They complement each other but are different concepts.

entries.title: Privileged vs. Unprivileged Container
paragraphs: If elevated host access is unnecessary, an unprivileged container is safer.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Verify every access request → Zero Trust

Provider's secure settings → Vendor-specific benchmark

Protect moving data → Encryption in transit
Protect stored data → Encryption at rest
Protect credentials or keys → Secrets management
Protect application interface → API security

Elevated container rights → Privileged
Reduced container rights → Unprivileged
Publicly exposed objects → Object storage security issue
